newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus soars, U.S. airs concerns.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus soars, U.S. airs concerns.

text.p: Japan unveiled figures on Thursday showing its current account surplus rose sharply in January, prompting the United States to urge Tokyo to take steps to prevent its resurgence.
Japanese officials, however, said the surplus in the current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- was still on a declining trend.

The current account surplus grew more than four-fold to 150.7 billion yen ($1.24 billion) in January from 32.6 billion yen ($269 million) a year earlier, the first monthly increase in 17 months. The surplus in merchandise trade alone, however, fell 15.5 percent to 229.3 billion yen ($1.89 billion). The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
The surplus had fallen in December for a 16th consecutive month of year-on-year declines, but the pace of the drop slowed due to the yen's fall.

Economists said the surplus was likely to keep growing as the surplus in merchandise trade, a major component in the current account, is expected to start rising due to yen's weakening since mid-1995.
Data released on Wednesday showed a 53.3 percent jump in the custom-cleared trade surplus in the first 20 days of February.
A U.S. official in Tokyo said after the figures were released that Japan should take whatever steps were needed to make sure that the surplus does not balloon again.

"Starting around the fall of last year, the drop in Japan's global current account surplus began to bottom out -- appeared to begin to bottom out -- and there are some indications that it might be turning around," Lawrence Greenwood, economic minister-counselor at the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo, told a news conference, adding that some private forecasters expected the surplus to rise in 1997.

"Japan needs to maintain sustained domestic demand-led growth and needs to take steps to avoid a resurgence of the current account surplus," he said, echoing recent comments by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.

Some analysts, however, predicted that the United States would focus more on trade ties with China this year than on Japan. "I think this has basically passed its sell-by date as a sexy market issue. The U.S. is now on the verge of taking trade problems with China more seriously," said Jane Berryman, a senior analyst at Technical Data, Tokyo.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary panel that Japan's current account surplus was not expected to rise substantially due to structural changes in its economy.

The yen's rise until April 1995 encouraged Japanese firms to shift production abroad, which in turn helped slow overall exports and boosted imports of products such as cars made overseas at Japanese-owned plants.
"The tempo (of the fall) will slow down, but the shrinking trend of the current account surplus remains unchanged," a ministry official told reporters.

The ministry official attributed the rise in the January current account surplus mostly to a fall in the deficit in services, which shrank about 12 percent to 513.7 billion yen ($4.25 billion). The smaller services deficit was due mainly to a rise in Japanese firms' income earned from overseas dealings in such commodities as oil and nonferrous metals.
Also contributing to the rise in the January current account surplus was a 26 percent rise in net income from Japanese investment in overseas securities.
